text: Lesson 13 laid out the five pieces every correlation rule needs: event source, condition, time window, threshold, and action. This lesson turns that shape into one real, vendor-neutral correlation rule, written in plain logical form instead of any one SIEM's exact query syntax, then walks through what each clause actually watches for.

The classic brute-force-then-success rule groups Windows Security Event Log logon events by user account, then fires when at least 5 logon-failure events land within a 10-minute window for that account, followed by a logon-success event for that same account inside that same window. The logic reads the same whether it's written in Splunk SPL, Microsoft Sentinel KQL, or any other SIEM's rule-building interface — only the syntax changes, not the reasoning.

The grouping key — here, user account — is what ties individual events into one coherent pattern instead of five unrelated people mistyping passwords. The threshold and time window work together: at least 5 matching failures, all inside the same 10 minutes. And the success condition has to apply to that exact same grouping key, inside that same window, which is what separates a real guess-and-land from ordinary unrelated typos.

Notice the rule also cares about order, not just count. Five failures in a row immediately followed by a success matches the pattern a brute-force guess would produce. One failure, a success, then four more unrelated failures from someone fat-fingering something else entirely does not — even though it has the same number of failures and one success inside the same window.

A rule that only counts events in a window, without checking what order they occurred in, would fire on both of those patterns — and the second one is almost always benign. Sequence-aware logic is what keeps a correlation rule aimed at actual attacker behavior instead of just raw event volume.
Next, Lesson 15 covers what happens once a rule like this one actually goes live: new rules almost always fire too often at first, and tuning is the real process that brings them under control.
